messages.body_plain:
I want to respond to this question as it seemed like it would be good to keep threads on this topic together. I am working on large scale report generation in knitr where at any one time I could be generating hundreds of reports based off of various geographies in a large scale database. The reports individually take about 5 minutes to run. If I wanted to run a report on every county in the US that is about 3,000 counties in total.

I am using a method not unsimilar to this one here:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/15396755/using-loops-with-knitr-to-produce-multiple-pdf-reports-need-a-little-help-to

Basically you loop through a Rnw file (document class is report in LaTex) to create many different pdfs.

library("knitr")
for (hosp in unique(df$Hospital)){
  knit2pdf("testingloops.Rnw", output=paste0('report_', hosp, '.tex'))
}
Generally I'm querying the relational database a bunch and drawing maps, plots, xtables, etc.

I tried simply replacing the for loop with a foreach loop (and executing via %dopar%) based on a doMC parallel backend. This process seems to work very slowly mostly because I think it is gathering the results and communicating them back to the original R file. So something like this:

library("knitr")
foreach (i=1:nrow(unique(df$County)){
  knit2pdf("testingloops.Rnw", output=paste0('report_', unique(df$County)[i], '.tex'))
}
I'm wondering:

1. Is it even worth it to actually parallelize the reports or just to run the loops as chunks on different machines
2. Am I not using some of the foreach combine arguments correctly.

This question I think is unique. I'm not really trying to do parallel computation inside a knitr document. I am trying to parallelize teh creation of many knitr documents. Does this make sense?

messages.body_plain:
But... this actually is not the same topic, since the original message had nothing about foreach, and it was knitting a single report together.

Regardless, parallel processing is not a panacea for making things go faster... it is targeted at things that need more cpu specifically. Having multiple processes fighting over I/O resources (database access, filesystem access, graphics device access, RAM access) is not a good way to speed things up. If your reports take a lot of cpu time and not too much RAM then you might get a boost, but it doesn't sound like that is the case for you. Even switching to using only one process per machine might not help if network access to your database is saturated. Profiling the generation of one report might be useful for understanding what you are up against.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm using texreg() to generate LaTeX tables within knitr.

This works ok when I use the raw code, but I am running a number of regressions on two subsets of data (Intention To Treat (ITT); Per-Protocol (PP)) for a primary outcome and a number of secondary outcomes as well.

The logical thing to me to do was to wrap my regression models and subsequent calls to texreg() into a function and then call that with the relevant outcome and subset of data.  To this end I have written (with some assistance <http://stackoverflow.com/a/24854036/1444043>)...

pleasant.regression <- function(data       = proportion,
                                time.frame = "September 2013",
                                outcome    = "unscheduled",
                                family     = binomial,
                                caption    = "ITT and PP Linear Mixed Effects Model Coefficients and Standard Errors for \\emph{any} Unscheduled Visits in September 2013.",
                                label    = "logistic-unscheduled",
                                ...){
    ## Require packages
    require(lme4)
    require(ResourceSelection)
    require(texreg)
    ## Set defaults for texreg tables, can be modified with additional arguments

    texreg.digits        <- 2
    texreg.table         <- TRUE
    texreg.caption.above <- TRUE
    texreg.booktabs      <- TRUE
    texreg.dcolumn       <- TRUE
    texreg.use.packages  <- FALSE
    texreg.float.pos     <- "!htpb"
    texreg.ci.force      <- TRUE
    texreg.ci.test       <- 0
    ## Parse the outcome into a formula with the desired mixed
    ## effects model
    .formula <- reformulate(response = outcome, termlabels = c("allocation", "gender", "age", "n.unscheduled.2012", "(1 | pracid)"))
    ## Logistic Regresion
    if(family == "binomial"){
        ## ITT
        itt.mixed <- lmer(.formula,
                          data   = subset(data,
                                          period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE),
                          family = family)
        ## PP
        pp.mixed <- lmer(.formula,
                         data   = subset(data,
                                         period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE & pp == 1),
                         family = family)
    }
    ## Negative Binomial
    else if(family == "negbin"){
        ## ITT
        itt.mixed <- glmer.nb(.formula,
                              data   = subset(data,
                                              period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE))
        ## PP
        pp.mixed <- glmer.nb(.formula,
                             data   = subset(data,
                                             period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE & pp == 1))
    }
    ## Save table comparing ITT to PP using texreg()
    results <- paste(capture.output(texreg(list(itt.mixed, pp.mixed),
                                    custom.model.names = c("ITT", "PP"),
                                    custom.coef.names  = c("Intercept", "Allocation (Letter)", "Gender (Female)", "Age", "$N_{Unscheduled}$ September 2012"),
                                    digits             = texreg.digits,
                                    caption            = caption,
                                    table              = texreg.table,
                                    caption.above      = texreg.caption.above,
                                    label              = label,
                                    booktabs           = texreg.booktabs,
                                    dcolumn            = texreg.dcolumn,
                                    use.packages       = texreg.use.packages,
                                    float.pos          = texreg.float.pos,
                                    ci.force           = texreg.ci.force,
                                    ci.test            = texreg.ci.test)),
                     collapse="\n")
    return(results)
}

    ## Set defaults for texreg

    texreg.caption.above <- TRUE
    texreg.booktabs      <- TRUE
    texreg.dcolumn       <- TRUE
    texreg.use.packages  <- FALSE
    texreg.float.pos     <- "!htpb"
    texreg.ci.force      <- TRUE

    ## Parse the outcome into a formula with the desired mixed
    ## effects model
    .formula <- reformulate(response = outcome, termlabels = c("allocation", "gender", "age", "n.unscheduled.2012", "(1 | pracid)"))
    ## Logistic Regresion
    if(family == "binomial"){
        ## ITT
        itt.mixed <- lmer(.formula,
                          data   = subset(data,
                                          period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE),
                          family = family)
        ## PP

                                         period == time.frame & age.include == TRUE & pp == 1),

        ## ITT

    results <- paste(capture.output(texreg(list(itt.mixed, pp.mixed),

                                           float.pos          = texreg.float.pos,

    ## Return the results

}

I've been thinking about how this arose and I've realised how I came to make this mistake.

I had originally written the code as an .R file that was read with read_chunk() and within that I re-sourced the custom extract.lme4.R.

I'd seen the error messages in my resulting PDF (its red and quite hard to miss) but hadn't been able to work out what was causing them and it wasn't a show stopper at the time with regards to the finished product since the subsequent analyses ran fine and my texreg() results table was displayed (my primary concern due to a pending meeting that required the results, that meeting has past and I can now focus on streamlining the code and writing repetitive chunks as functions).

As a consequence when turning it into a function I purposefully left the souce("scripts/extract.lme4.R") call in the newly defined function, thinking that because I had require(texreg) I had better re-source the modification, but as I've found thank to your direction Yihui, since the file wasn't being found it prevents the remainder of the function from executing.

A lesson learned for myself.  I'll be sure to bear this in mind when converting code to functions.

Thanks again,

Neil

messages.body_plain:
The standard latex classes (article, book, and report) accepts only 3
different font sizes: 10pt, 11pt, and 12pt.

(I suppose the the rmarkdown documentation could make that more
obvious https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/master/R/pdf_document.R#L53)

You'll need to use a custom latex class if you want size 24pt font.
(You may also look into telling rmarkdown to use xelatex, but you'll
still need to adjust the class).

Cheers,

Carl

That is not (yet) possible with knitr::kable(), but I think it should be easy to define your own function to do this, e.g.

format_thou = function(data, cols) {
  if (missing(cols)) {
    cols = NULL
    for (j in 1:ncol(data)) if (is.numeric(data[, j])) cols = c(cols, j)
  }
  if (length(cols))
    data[, cols] = format(data[, cols], big.mark = ',', scientific = FALSE)
  data
}
